title: How big is too big?
author: Less-Negotiation1022
selftext: Innuendo aside, how big is too big for a game developed entirely with AI? I'm creating a game based on my area in London. It covers a 3km radius with an insane amount of playable things. Almost every building apart from the homes has some sort of game feature. I'm really particular with details and the ideas do not stop. When is enough enough? I've been at it for 3 months and the features I want to implement kind of get implemented with ease. I see a lot of people pumping out 5 prompt games and people seem to love it. Is being a perfectionist going to hurt me? Is keeping it simple good enough in a saturated market of mostly slop with gems dotted around? I have people really interested in this game. Feeling the pressure 🤣

comments.author: horsewitnoname
comments.body:
I’m making a city-sized map with over 2,000 buildings and every one of them will be enters or and fully furnished. It’s taking a while, but it’s really fun to get Claude going on something and waking up in the morning to see the progress it has made with 8 hours of uninterrupted work time. 

It’s insanely impressive tbh.

comments.author: ziptofaf
comments.body:
It's not about size but about coherence of your setting. Adding random game features usually does NOT help for instance. If anything it can be harmful long term as you are piling up width but not depth of the experience.

Of course, there are exceptions. Goat Simulator is a good example of width over depth. It's insane, it's a short adventure and you have all kinds of random nonsense inside. There's certainly market for it.

>Is being a perfectionist going to hurt me?

Just adding more stuff doesn't make the game better. The important part is your core gameplay loop. Size may be useful when it adds to it but it's never a primary factor. Usually games are iterated upon - you start from a single room and a single mechanic, then once you are satisfied you add another small part. And eventually you have a game.

So before I can tell you whether your choice is good or bad - well, what's your game about and who is your target audience? What other games do they play? Cuz it's not possible to rate anything that you are doing without this information. 3x3x3.14 is not a metric games are judged by. I mean - it's either 30% of GTA VI or like 3x Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Or at least 3 Doom Eternals. Or 0.01% of Daggerfall.

replies.author: Less-Negotiation1022
replies.body: So it's an underground London mafia story based around deep corruption at its core. A coherent consistent story that progresses through missions and scenes. You can play both as the hero and villain. That is a part of it. There's also an open world with multiple different characters who have different jobs to acquire money according to their personality. Each experience with the map is different depending on your character. Every character starts with NOTHING and it's a barbaric harsh world out there. My target audience is for people who are crying out for a London based game. I loved The Getaway Black Monday and no-one has recaptured that magic since.

comments.body: Its about quality not quantity but no such thing as too big, but if things are shallow or repetitive then thats the opposite. Im not sure if ur game is 3d or 2d but like is the content actually fun and engaging or not is the question.

comments.author: YeetCompleet
comments.body:
"insane amount of playable things"

Elaborate. Cohesiveness matters more than insane amounts of things. Even in games like Mario Party, there is overall structural cohesiveness and thematic cohesiveness holding the minigames together.

replies.author: Less-Negotiation1022
replies.body: You can hit up an underground weed cafe and physically grind weed and smoke a joint. This increases your creativity and with enough creativity you can unlock things like a studio session with Suno integrated for your character to make a song and then you can market this song via virtual social media stored on your phone and depending on success you earn money. There's a playable TopGolf course with points system. Every area of the map where there is some sort of sports pitch, you can play that sport but a unique version of it with rewards for your character based on victory and difficulty level. So you can kinda understand how this is going

comments.body: “everything” games will be big in 2027, you need to shit or get off pot

comments.author: YouKnowItsMeStudios
comments.body:
Do yourself a huge favor, if you haven't already, write yourself a document now of everything you want the first release to have and stick to it.

Any ideas you have after that go in a separate doc for future additions.

Scope creep is real and will easily turn a year of dev work into three just to get the first release out.

comments.author: dr0idattack137
comments.body: Somebody told me you might have to actually remove things to make a cohesive game.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: The Yakuza games have pretty small maps but are very dense with different minigames and events happening pretty much every screen, and they're highly regarded. For a solo dev, it's probably better to go smaller unless the actual movement is meaningful and distance is required, but otherwise you're basically beholden to that whole 3km map now, you have to ensure that every block looks good, everything looks consistent, there are enough characters to fill out the spaces so they don't look empty (this is London afterall), and so on. It's a ton of effort for an environment team over years, let alone a single dev.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Start small, if it's not fun, big won't help. 

I'm building a big game too but you need to scale it. My world is supposed to be 60*60km but you need to start small and optimize along the way otherwise you run into so many problems that will burn you out
